headline.statement: In all six models of the paper's main results table, the mediation's key coefficient -- the effect of emotion dysregulation on loss-of-control eating -- is printed under a row label describing a completely different two-step pathway, and that same label appears a second time lower in the same block carrying different numbers.
headline.evidence: Table 2, Model 1, under the heading 'Direct effects', prints five rows: 'Negative affect ➔ Emotion dysregulation' 0.35 (0.06); 'Positive affect ➔ Emotion dysregulation' -0.07 (0.03); 'Positive affect ➔ Emotion dysregulation ➔ LOC eating' 0.28 (0.07), p < 0.001, β = 0.13, and between-person 0.82 (0.41), p = 0.048, β = 0.68; 'Negative affect ➔ LOC eating' -0.05 (0.12); 'Positive affect ➔ LOC eating' 0.06 (0.07). The third row cannot be a direct effect -- it names a two-step path -- and the identical label reappears under 'Indirect effects' in the same model with different values, -0.02 (0.01), p = 0.070. The body text assigns those exact numbers to the missing path: 'significant positive associations between the emotion dysregulation factors relative to the general sense of LOC while eating and feelings of disconnection ... at both the within-person (β = 0.13–0.14) and between-person (β = 0.68–0.77) levels', matching Model 1 (0.13/0.68) and Model 6 (0.14/0.77).
headline.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a contradiction between a printed row label, the structure a mediation model must have, and the paper's own body text. The underlying values were verified with: metascience regression-batch --rows '[{"label":"T2 M1 W b-path","b":0.28,"se":0.07,"reported_p":0.001,"p_is_threshold":true,"decimals_b":2,"decimals_se":2,"decimals_p":3,"df":100000,"df_source":"assumed"}]'
headline.plain: The paper's central question is whether difficulty managing emotions is the link between how someone feels and their loss of control over eating. The single most important number in that chain -- how strongly emotion difficulty predicts loss-of-control eating -- is printed in the main table under a heading that names a different chain of events entirely, and the same heading is used again a few rows below for different numbers. The numbers themselves are correct and match what the text describes; it is the labels that are wrong, in all six of the paper's models. A reader working only from the table would misunderstand which result is which.

findings.title: Table 2's key mediation coefficient is printed under a label naming a different pathway, in all six models
findings.location: Table 2, 'Direct effects' block, third row of all six models
findings.reported: Row printed as 'Positive affect ➔ Emotion dysregulation ➔ LOC eating' under the heading 'Direct effects'. Model 1: 0.28 (0.07), p < 0.001, β = 0.13 within-person; 0.82 (0.41), p = 0.048, β = 0.68 between-person. Model 6: 0.25 (0.06), p < 0.001, β = 0.14; 1.00 (0.41), p = 0.014, β = 0.77.
findings.computed: The row must be the b-path, emotion dysregulation ➔ LOC eating. Three independent confirmations, all read at source from the XML table grid: (1) a 1-1-1 mediation has exactly five direct paths and the block prints exactly five rows, the other four correctly labelled, leaving only ED➔LOC unaccounted for; (2) a two-step path cannot by definition sit under 'Direct effects'; (3) the Results section headed 'Emotion Dysregulation (M) ➔ LOC Eating (Y)' reports β = 0.13–0.14 within-person and β = 0.68–0.77 between-person, which are exactly the Model 1 and Model 6 values in this row. The identical label also already occupies a row in the Indirect effects block of every model, carrying different values.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The reading rests on the structure of the mediation model the paper describes in its Methods and on the values printed in its own Results text; no external range or bound was supplied. All values were re-read directly from the publisher XML table grid, which carried no alignment_uncertain or image_only flag.
findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a cross-reference contradiction between a printed row label, the model structure, and the body text.

consequence.explanation: The emotion-dysregulation-to-LOC-eating direct effect, which the Results discuss at length as β = 0.13–0.14 within-person and 0.68–0.77 between-person, is mislabelled in all six models of the paper's only results table.

findings.plain: In the main results table, the row carrying the paper's most important finding is given the wrong name -- it is described as a two-step chain when it is actually a single step, and the very same description is used again lower down for a different result. The numbers are right and agree with the written description in the text, so no conclusion changes; but anyone reading the table on its own would attribute the paper's headline result to the wrong pathway.

findings.title: Claimed variation across loss-of-control eating dimensions rests on comparing significance verdicts, not on testing the difference
findings.location: Results, Indirect Effects paragraph; Discussion, 'Variations Across LOC Eating Dimensions'; Table 2, Models 1–6 within-person indirect effects
findings.reported: 'The emotion dysregulation factors did not mediate associations between the negative affect factors and either the difficulties stopping eating after starting or the not paying attention to one's eating factors'. The Discussion builds on this: 'there was greater variability in whether moment-to-moment changes in the two self-regulatory factors promoted this LOC eating outcome', with substantive explanations offered (others entering the room, alternative coping behaviours). Model 3 within-person indirect effect: 0.04 (0.03), p = 0.154, against significant effects of 0.10 (0.03), 0.09 (0.03) and 0.09 (0.03) in Models 1, 4 and 6.
findings.computed: A 95% Wald interval derived from the printed b and SE for the Model 3 null is [-0.019, 0.099]. The largest effect this null is compatible with, 0.099, is as large as or larger than all three of the indirect effects the paper reports as significant (0.10, 0.09, 0.09). The paper states no smallest effect size of interest anywhere, so equivalence cannot be tested and no conclusion of 'no effect' is licensed. No test of the difference between dimensions is reported.
findings.assumptions: The interval is derived by this review from the paper's printed coefficient and standard error on the normal distribution, not printed by the authors -- the paper reports no confidence intervals for any coefficient. It inherits the two-decimal rounding of the printed values. The inferential point (that a significant and a non-significant result are not thereby different from each other) is the difference-in-significance fallacy described by Gelman and Stern, 2006, The American Statistician 60:328-331.

consequence.explanation: The paper's second stated aim -- that mediation varies across LOC eating dimensions -- and the Discussion section built on it rest on contrasting significant with non-significant pathways whose plausible effect ranges overlap almost entirely.

findings.plain: One of the paper's two main conclusions is that emotional difficulty matters for some kinds of loss-of-control eating but not others. The evidence for that is simply that some results passed the usual statistical significance cut-off and others did not. But a result that misses the cut-off is not thereby shown to be zero: for the two dimensions called non-mediated, the data are still compatible with an effect just as large as the ones the paper calls significant. To claim the dimensions genuinely differ, the authors would need to test the difference between them directly, which they do not do. The first conclusion -- that emotional difficulty mediates the effect of negative mood on several eating dimensions -- is not affected by this and remains supported.

findings.title: One of the four significant mediation pathways does not survive correction for the twelve tests it belongs to
findings.location: Table 2, Indirect effects rows, within-person columns (12 tests); abstract and Conclusions
findings.reported: Twelve within-person indirect effects (two predictors crossed with six LOC eating dimensions), p = 0.001, 0.026, 0.154, 0.001, 0.858, 0.001, 0.070, 0.122, 0.233, 0.067, 0.859, 0.065. Table 2 note: 'Bold text is used to reflect significant effects, defined as p < 0.05'. No correction for multiple comparisons is stated anywhere in the paper.
findings.computed: Twelve uncorrected tests at alpha = 0.05 imply a family-wise error rate up to 46.0% and about 0.6 false positives by chance. Four results are significant uncorrected; exactly 3 survive under all four corrections (Bonferroni threshold 0.0042, Holm 0.0050, Benjamini-Hochberg 0.0125, Benjamini-Yekutieli 0.0040). The claim lost is the difficulties-resisting-eating pathway at p = 0.026. The three pathways at p = 0.001 survive every correction including Benjamini-Yekutieli, which is the appropriate one here because the LOC dimensions are strongly correlated (Table S.2 reports momentary covariances of 0.66–0.73 among four of them).
findings.assumptions: What counts as a family is my judgement, not the tool's: I took the paper's own primary claim set -- one stated aim, the same 107 participants, two predictors crossed with six outcomes. Uncorrected testing at this scale is entirely ordinary in the ecological momentary assessment literature and this is arithmetic about what the numbers imply, not an accusation. The paper never promised to correct, so this is a standard I am supplying. Twelve is a floor on the true comparison count: the exploratory analyses add twenty-four further tests of the reversed pathway.
findings.reproduction: metascience multiplicity --family-label "Within-person indirect effects, 2 predictors x 6 LOC dimensions, Table 2" --tests '[{"p_value":0.001},{"p_value":0.026},{"p_value":0.154},{"p_value":0.001},{"p_value":0.858},{"p_value":0.001},{"p_value":0.07},{"p_value":0.122},{"p_value":0.233},{"p_value":0.067},{"p_value":0.859},{"p_value":0.065}]' --alpha 0.05

consequence.explanation: The within-person indirect effect on difficulties resisting eating (p = 0.026) crosses back over alpha under every standard correction, yet is presented in the Results and Conclusions on equal footing with the three pathways that survive.

findings.plain: The authors ran twelve related statistical tests and counted any result below the usual one-in-twenty threshold as real, without adjusting for the fact that running twelve tests makes a chance finding much more likely -- there is roughly a 46% chance of at least one false alarm. Three of their four positive findings are strong enough to survive that adjustment comfortably. The fourth, concerning difficulty resisting eating, does not survive any standard adjustment, yet is reported alongside the others as an established result. Not adjusting is common practice in this field, so this is a caveat on one specific claim rather than a criticism of the analysis as a whole.

findings.title: "Participants without sufficient data did not differ" is asserted from comparisons against just five excluded people
findings.location: Methods, Participants and Procedures; Data S1, Table S.6
findings.reported: 'Participants without sufficient data did not differ from those in the analytic sample on baseline methodological (e.g., treatment group, treatment completion status), demographic (e.g., gender, BMI), or psychopathological factors'. Table S.6 compares n = 107 against n = 5. Baseline Beck Depression Inventory: d = 0.736, 95% CI -0.418 to 1.886, p = .212. Also age d = -0.591, BMI d = -0.563, DERS d = 0.453.
findings.computed: The BDI interval includes the null but remains compatible with the excluded participants being up to 1.886 standard deviations more depressed -- an enormous difference. The point estimate d = 0.736 is itself a large effect that is non-significant only because n = 5. Three further rows carry medium-to-large point estimates in the same position. No smallest effect size of interest is stated, so equivalence cannot be tested and no conclusion of 'no difference' is licensed. Separately, the chi-squared tests on gender and treatment completion status have expected cell counts far below 5 in the excluded group, violating the chi-squared approximation.
findings.assumptions: The interval is the one the paper itself prints for Cohen's d, so no bound was supplied by this review. Nothing here suggests anything improper: 5 exclusions out of 112 is a good retention rate and the authors were right to check. The objection is only that the check as performed cannot support the flat assertion the Methods draw from it.

consequence.explanation: The Methods assertion that excluded and included participants did not differ is not established by these intervals, which remain compatible with large baseline differences in depression, age and BMI.

findings.plain: Five of the 112 people enrolled were dropped from the analysis for having too little data. The authors checked whether those five differed from the rest and reported that they did not. With only five people, such a check can barely detect anything: the results remain compatible with the excluded five being dramatically more depressed than those kept, and the best estimate actually points that way. The honest summary is that comparability could not be established, not that it was established. This does not indicate anything improper -- keeping 107 of 112 participants is good -- but the reassurance the sentence offers is not backed by the numbers behind it.

findings.title: The emotion dysregulation factor structure is described as "confirmed" on fit statistics from a model that cannot fail
findings.location: Methods, Emotion Dysregulation; Data S1, Table S.1, Emotion Dysregulation row
findings.reported: 'The factor structure was confirmed via MCFA in the present sample following minor modifications (see Data S1).' Table S.1 prints for Emotion Dysregulation: χ² (df) = 0.034 (0), p = 1.000, CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.000, RMSEA = 0.000, SRMR within = 0.000, between = 0.001. The two rows above it, Negative Affect 69.690 (10) and Positive Affect 26.657 (4), are informative by contrast.
findings.computed: df = 0 means the model is just-identified (saturated): it has as many free parameters as observed moments and reproduces the data exactly by construction. CFI = 1.000, TLI = 1.000 and RMSEA = 0.000 are the values a saturated model must return whatever the data are, and therefore carry no information about whether the factor structure is correct. No p-value can be computed from a chi-squared at df = 0, which is the point.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed degrees of freedom, read directly from the supplementary table. An innocent reading is available and may well be right: the authors may report the row for completeness rather than as evidence. The paper does not distinguish it from the two informative rows printed immediately above it, and the Methods sentence cites the MCFA as the confirmation.
findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a reading of the reported degrees of freedom. recalc_stat_to_p cannot convert a chi-squared at df = 0, which is itself the finding.

consequence.explanation: The claim that the emotion dysregulation factor structure was confirmed by factor analysis is not supported by the fit statistics reported for it, and emotion dysregulation is the mediator in all six primary models.

findings.plain: Before running their main analysis, the authors checked that their questionnaire measures behave as intended, and report that the emotion-difficulty measure passed. But the particular model they fitted for that measure had no room to fail: it has exactly as many adjustable settings as pieces of information, so it always fits perfectly regardless of what the data look like. The perfect scores reported beside it are therefore automatic and tell a reader nothing. This matters because emotion difficulty is the pivot of every model in the paper, and because the authors say this was the one measure that needed adjusting before it fitted.

findings.title: The only covariate carried into all twelve models falls below the paper's own stated inclusion threshold
findings.location: Data S1, Missing Data Analyses text and Table S.7
findings.reported: 'Meaningful/influential covariates were determined using Cohen's (1988) recommendations for small (R2 = 0.02), medium (R2 = 0.13), and large (R2 = 0.26) effects. Effects that were small to medium sized or larger (i.e., R2 ≥ 0.03), were considered influential.' And: 'the data were generally shown to be missing at random relative to the survey number of the day (1-6; R2s = 0.029)'. Every other covariate returns 0.000 or 0.002.
findings.computed: 0.029 < 0.030, so the sole covariate carried into all six primary and six exploratory models falls below the paper's own stated inclusion rule. The rule also does not follow from the benchmark cited in the sentence immediately before it, which gives 'small' as R2 = 0.02, not 0.03.
findings.assumptions: Both numbers are quoted verbatim from the supplement and were re-read at source. Two innocent readings are available and either may be right: the authors may have applied a >= 0.02 rule consistent with the benchmark they cite and mis-transcribed it as 0.03, or 0.029 may be a rounded display of a value at or above 0.030. Both would be transcription rather than analytic errors. Note also that 0.02/0.13/0.26 are Cohen's benchmarks for f-squared rather than R-squared, though this usage is common in practice.
findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a contradiction between a stated decision rule and its application, established by comparing two printed numbers.

consequence.explanation: The stated covariate-selection rule, as printed, excludes the survey-number covariate that was in fact included in all twelve models.

findings.plain: The authors set themselves a rule for deciding which background variables were important enough to adjust for, and stated the cut-off as a specific number. The one variable they went on to adjust for in every model scores just below that cut-off -- 0.029 against a stated 0.03. The rule as written also does not match the published benchmark the authors cite one sentence earlier. Most likely one of the two numbers is a typing slip, but as printed the paper's own rule excludes the variable it was used to justify including.

findings.title: Reported EMA compliance of 70.00% does not match the count and denominator printed beside it
findings.reported: 'Participants responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%).'
findings.computed: 3131/4494 = 69.67%, outside the rounding interval [69.995, 70.01] that a figure printed as 70.00 asserts. The printed percentage implies a denominator of about 4473 rather than 4494. The denominator itself is internally coherent: 107 participants x 6 surveys x 7 days = 4494, built on the analytic sample rather than the 112 enrolled (which would give 4704).
findings.assumptions: The quoted sentence was re-read verbatim in the body text. The most likely innocent explanation, and one I cannot rule out, is that 70.00% is the mean of participants' individual compliance rates rather than the pooled ratio printed beside it -- these differ whenever compliance varies across participants, and reporting the mean of individual rates is standard in this literature. The paper does not say which it reports. Presentational rounding of 69.67% is a second possibility. Either way, three numbers printed in one sentence do not reconcile with each other.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the descriptive characterisation of EMA compliance as 'good'; no inferential result in Table 2 depends on this figure.

findings.plain: The paper says participants answered 3131 of 4494 possible surveys, which it describes as 70.00% compliance. Those two numbers actually give 69.67%. The likeliest explanation is harmless -- the 70.00% is probably the average of each person's individual response rate rather than the overall total, which is a normal way to report this -- but as written the sentence contains three figures that do not add up together. Nothing in the paper's results depends on it.

findings.title: Predictor and mediator roles for the exploratory models are stated backwards in two places
findings.location: Data S1, Table S.5 note; Results, Exploratory Analyses paragraph
findings.reported: Table S.5 is titled 'Model Fit Statistics for the Exploratory Multilevel Structural Equation Models Examining Momentary Associations among Emotion Dysregulation (Predictor), Negative and Positive Affect (Mediators), and Loss of Control Eating Dimensions (Outcomes)', but its own note reads 'all models included negative affect and positive affect factors as predictors, the emotion dysregulation factor as a mediator, and the loss of control eating items shown in column 1 as outcomes'. Separately, the Results state 'nor were any pathways involving positive affect as a predictor', describing models in which positive affect is the mediator.
findings.computed: The title and the note beneath it assign the two roles in opposite directions; both were read verbatim at source. Table S.4, which carries the exploratory coefficients themselves, labels the paths in the direction the title gives, so the models were evidently run as the title describes and only the note and the Results sentence are wrong. The substantive claim the Results sentence makes is correct regardless: all twelve exploratory pathways involving positive affect are non-significant.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own printed text. Most plausibly the footnote was copied from the corresponding primary-model fit table, where the assignment is correct, and the Results sentence carried over from the parallel sentence about the primary analyses, where 'predictor' is also correct.
findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a contradiction between a table's own title and its own footnote, and between the Results text and the supplementary table it describes.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the description of which models the exploratory fit statistics belong to; the statistics themselves are distinct from the primary models' and are evidently the exploratory ones.

findings.plain: The paper runs a second set of models with the causal chain reversed, to see whether the results hold in the other direction. In two places the description of which variable plays which role in those reversed models is stated the wrong way round -- once in a table's footnote, which contradicts that same table's own title, and once in the text. The actual analyses appear to have been done correctly; only the descriptions are wrong. Taken with the mislabelled row in the main table, this suggests the tables were assembled by copying and editing rows without a final consistency check.

findings.title: The trial registration number printed in the Methods has seven digits and cannot resolve
findings.reported: 'The present study used baseline EMA data from a multisite randomized controlled trial (NCT0204349) testing the efficacy of Integrative Cognitive-Affective Therapy (ICAT-BED) versus guided self-help Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Eating Disorders (CBTgsh).'
findings.computed: ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers are the letters NCT followed by exactly eight digits. The printed value has seven, so as given it does not resolve to any registration.
findings.assumptions: The eight-digit NCT format is an external convention of the ClinicalTrials.gov registry, not something the paper states. This is almost certainly a dropped digit rather than anything substantive -- the parent trial plainly exists and is cited to Peterson et al. (2020) -- and I make no suggestion otherwise. I flag it because this is the one sentence a reader would use to locate the protocol, and because the paper reports no prespecification for its own secondary analyses, so the registration is the only available route to that judgement.
findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a format check on a printed registry identifier.

consequence.explanation: Prevents a reader from retrieving the parent trial's registration, which is the only available basis for judging whether these secondary analyses were prespecified.

findings.plain: The paper gives a registration number for the parent clinical trial so readers can look up the original study plan. The number as printed is one digit short of the required length, so it does not lead anywhere. This is almost certainly a typing slip and the trial clearly exists, but it does close off the only route a reader has to check whether these particular analyses were planned in advance or decided after seeing the data.

findings.title: No degrees of freedom, no observation-level sample size, and two-decimal coefficients leave the main results table unverifiable
findings.location: Table 2 (84 coefficients) and Data S1 Table S.4 (24 coefficients checked); Methods, LOC Eating
findings.reported: Table 2 prints b (SE) to two decimals with a separate p column, for coefficients whose magnitude is often 0.01–0.02 -- for example Model 6's within-person positive-affect indirect effect, -0.02 (0.01), p = 0.065. No degrees of freedom appear anywhere in the article or supplement. The paper reports 3131 completed surveys but never the number of observations entering any model; LOC eating items were shown only after a reported eating episode, and predictors were lagged twice and mediators once with no lagging across days or missed surveys.
findings.computed: All 108 checked coefficients reconcile with their own standard error and p-value at any degrees of freedom from 30 upward, which covers every value plausible for this design; 0 are inconsistent. The result is nonetheless clamped to indeterminate rather than reported as clean, because the df is this review's assumption and the verdict changes at df = 10. Separately, two-decimal rounding leaves small coefficients unconstrained: b in [0.015, 0.025] over se in [0.005, 0.015] admits a test statistic anywhere from 1.0 to 5.0, so none of the twelve within-person indirect effects can be independently checked from Table 2 as printed. The supplement's Table S.4 prints the same class of quantity to three decimals, which is sufficient.
findings.assumptions: The degrees of freedom used in the check were assumed by this review, not printed by the paper, and the batch was re-run across df = 10, 30, 100 and 100000 for that reason. Indirect-effect p-values in multilevel structural equation models may come from a delta-method or bootstrap procedure rather than a Wald test, in which case exact agreement with b/SE is not required. Reporting the level-1 N is good practice whose absence is common; I flag it here because it is the specific thing preventing verification.
findings.reproduction: metascience regression-batch --rows '[{"label":"M1 W NA->ED","b":0.35,"se":0.06,"reported_p":0.001,"p_is_threshold":true,"decimals_b":2,"decimals_se":2,"decimals_p":3,"df":100000,"df_source":"assumed"},{"label":"S4 M1 W ind NA","b":0.122,"se":0.046,"reported_p":0.008,"decimals_b":3,"decimals_se":3,"decimals_p":3,"df":100000,"df_source":"assumed"}]'

consequence.explanation: None of the twelve within-person indirect effects in Table 2 can be independently recomputed from the values printed for them, and the observation count underlying every within-person estimate is not reported.

findings.plain: Nothing here is wrong -- every one of the 108 coefficients I could check agrees with the numbers printed beside it. The problem is that three pieces of information needed to check them independently are missing: how many observations each model actually used, a technical quantity needed to convert test statistics into probabilities, and enough decimal places on the smallest coefficients. For results as small as 0.02, rounding to two decimal places leaves so much slack that an outside reader cannot confirm the reported probability at all. The supplement prints the equivalent numbers to three decimals, which is enough; the main table does not.

findings.title: An exploratory pathway counted as significant at p = .049 recomputes to p = .051 from its own printed values
findings.location: Data S1, Table S.4, Model 6, within-person indirect effect of emotion dysregulation via negative affect
findings.reported: 'Emotion Dysregulation à Negative Affect à LOC Eating   0.076 (0.039)   .049   0.039', printed in bold, which the table note defines as significant at p < .05.
findings.computed: The point estimate 0.076/0.039 gives t = 1.949 and p = .0513. The reported p = .049 nonetheless lies inside the interval [.047, .056] that the printed b and SE permit once their own rounding is taken into account, so the check passes and no discrepancy is alleged.
findings.assumptions: No error is claimed. The innocent reading -- that the authors hold the unrounded values and .049 is correct -- is the likely one, and the check reconciles via the printed-precision allowance rather than strictly. This is recorded as a fragility in one secondary claim, not as evidence of a mistake. Degrees of freedom were assumed as elsewhere.

consequence.explanation: One of the four exploratory pathways the paper reports as significant sits at the alpha boundary and cannot be independently confirmed as significant from the printed values.

findings.plain: One of the secondary findings is reported as just clearing the significance threshold, at .049 where .050 is the cut-off. Recomputing it from the two numbers printed next to it gives .051, just the other side. The gap is entirely explained by rounding, and the authors' figure is probably the correct one since they have the unrounded values -- but it means an outside reader cannot confirm that this particular result falls on the significant side.

findings.title: Data, code and the reported sensitivity analyses are available only on request, and the sensitivity results appear nowhere
findings.location: Data Availability Statement; Methods, LOC Eating
findings.reported: 'The data, material, and code that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.' Separately: 'Sensitivity analyses showed that the overall pattern of results was consistent when data from assessments that followed eating episodes only were used, and those in which non-eating and eating episodes were included'.
findings.computed: No data, materials or code are deposited; access is gated on a request judged reasonable by the authors. The sensitivity analyses the Methods report as having been run appear in neither the article nor the supplement, so that claim cannot be checked at all.
findings.assumptions: This is an extremely common statement in this literature, is frequently the journal's own default wording, and carries no suggestion of impropriety -- I record it at indeterminate for that reason. It is worth noting in this specific case only because several checks in this review returned indeterminate solely for want of the degrees of freedom and the unrounded coefficients, both of which would be immediately resolvable from the model output the statement covers.
findings.reproduction: No CLI command applies: this is a reporting-practice observation about the data availability statement and an absent analysis.

consequence.explanation: The sensitivity analyses the Methods rely on to justify the analytic choice of eating-episode-only data are reported as having been run but their results are not shown anywhere.

findings.plain: The underlying data and analysis code are not posted publicly; readers must ask the authors and be judged reasonable. That is standard practice and not a criticism in itself. It matters a little more than usual here because a handful of checks in this review could not be completed purely for want of two technical numbers that the authors' own analysis output would contain. Separately, the paper states it ran an additional robustness check and that the results held, but the results of that check are not shown anywhere, so a reader has to take it on trust.

triage.reason: Stage 1 had already stepped this down from the tool's `suspicious` and I agree it should not be carried at all: the printed p comes from an independent-samples t-test while the interval is a noncentral-t interval for Cohen's d, two different procedures that are not required to agree, and the 0.0015 residual is a standard reporting convention rather than a defect.

Downgraded from suspicious to indeterminate: this is the journal's standard availability wording and rulebook rule 7 aims at state-but-withhold in a suspicious context, which this is not; flagging a boilerplate statement as a defect would hold the paper to a standard it never accepted.

Merged into the reporting-sufficiency finding (rank 10) together with the coefficient-precision, supplement-S4 and level-1-N findings; all four are the same underlying defect -- the main results table cannot be independently recomputed -- and 0 of 108 coefficients were inconsistent, so this is not an accusation in its own right.

limitations: This agent reads text and does not see figures. The sweep's figure pass was run against the PDF and established that the paper contains exactly one figure, a conceptual path diagram of the mediation structure carrying no data values, so no numeric content was lost to figure-blindness in this case; but no figure was visually inspected at this stage.

Nine of nine accusations arrived from the sweep carrying a 'quote not located' marker. All nine were resolved at source in this stage: five were confirmed verbatim in the article body text, one in Table 2's own footnote, one in the Table 2 cell grid, and two in the supplementary Word document. The markers were an artefact of the locator searching the article XML for passages that live in table cells and in the supplement, not evidence that any value was mistranscribed.

Degrees of freedom are printed nowhere in the article or supplement, so every regression check here rests on a df this review assumed. The batches were re-run at df = 10, 30, 100 and 100000; all 108 coefficients reconcile from df = 30 upward and none is inconsistent, but the aggregate verdict is a refusal rather than a clean bill for that reason.

The multiplicity result depends on a family definition that is my judgement, not a computation. I took the paper's own primary claim set -- two predictors crossed with six outcomes on the same participants, matching its stated aim. A reader who defines the family differently will get a different number of surviving claims.

Effect-size plausibility could not be assessed: the benchmark table this system holds has no row for within-person mediation coefficients from ecological momentary assessment designs, so there is no citable comparison class against which to judge whether these indirect effects are unusual for the field.

The interval used to evaluate the paper's null claims was derived by this review from the printed coefficient and standard error, not printed by the authors. The paper reports no confidence interval for any coefficient in Table 2, so no interval here is the paper's own.

questions_for_authors.question: In Table 2, under the heading 'Direct effects', the third row of each of the six models is labelled 'Positive affect ➔ Emotion dysregulation ➔ LOC eating' and carries, for Model 1, 0.28 (0.07), p < 0.001, β = 0.13 within-person and 0.82 (0.41), p = 0.048, β = 0.68 between-person. The Results section reports the emotion dysregulation to LOC eating direct effect as β = 0.13–0.14 within-person and β = 0.68–0.77 between-person, and the same row label appears again in the Indirect effects block with different values. Could you confirm whether that row is in fact the emotion dysregulation ➔ LOC eating path?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles the headline finding directly; a one-word confirmation establishes whether this is a label error or something else.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you send the degrees of freedom and the observation-level (level 1) sample size for each of the twelve multilevel structural equation models, together with the unrounded coefficients and standard errors for the indirect effects in Table 2? Several of the smaller indirect effects are printed to two decimals (for example -0.02 (0.01), p = 0.065), which leaves the implied test statistic unconstrained.
questions_for_authors.why: Would convert roughly a dozen indeterminate refusals in this review into determinate checks, and is the single most useful thing that could be supplied.

questions_for_authors.question: The Results state that participants 'responded to 3131 out of 4494 possible surveys, reflecting good compliance (70.00%)', but 3131/4494 is 69.67%. Could you confirm whether the 70.00% figure is the mean of participants' individual compliance rates rather than the pooled ratio?
questions_for_authors.why: Distinguishes the likely benign explanation (mean of individual rates, standard in EMA reporting) from a transcription slip, and resolves the finding either way.

questions_for_authors.question: The supplement states that 'Effects that were small to medium sized or larger (i.e., R2 ≥ 0.03), were considered influential', while the preceding sentence gives Cohen's small-effect benchmark as R2 = 0.02, and the survey-number covariate that was carried into all twelve models is reported at R2 = 0.029. Could you clarify which threshold was applied?
questions_for_authors.why: As printed, the stated rule excludes the only covariate it was used to include; either the threshold or the R-squared is likely mis-transcribed and the authors can say which.

questions_for_authors.question: The Methods give the parent trial registration as NCT0204349, which has seven digits where ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers carry eight. Could you supply the full identifier?
questions_for_authors.why: The registration is the only available route to judging whether these secondary analyses were prespecified, and the identifier as printed does not resolve.

questions_for_authors.question: The Methods report that 'Sensitivity analyses showed that the overall pattern of results was consistent when data from assessments that followed eating episodes only were used, and those in which non-eating and eating episodes were included', but the results of those analyses do not appear in the article or in Data S1. Could you send them?
questions_for_authors.why: The choice to analyse eating-episode-only data rests on this comparison, and there is currently nothing a reader can check.

report_markdown:
This is a secondary analysis of baseline ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data from a multisite randomised trial of two treatments for binge eating disorder. One hundred and seven adults answered up to six brief surveys a day for a week. The authors fit six two-level structural equation models, each asking whether momentary emotion dysregulation carries the effect of momentary affect onto one of six distinct facets of loss-of-control (LOC) eating, and a further six exploratory models running the chain in reverse.

## What verified

Begin with the arithmetic, because on this paper almost all of it holds. Every one of the 108 coefficient triples I could check -- 84 in Table 2, 24 in supplementary Table S.4 -- reconciles with the standard error and p-value printed beside it, at any degrees of freedom from 30 upward, which spans every value plausible for this design. Not one is inconsistent. Every count in Table 1 reproduces its own percentage exactly at N = 107, fifteen cells out of fifteen. All three categorical blocks sum to exactly 107 with zero tolerance, and each percentage column sums to 99.99, inside its rounding window. The two model chi-squared statistics I converted reproduce their reported thresholds essentially exactly, as do the two attrition tests. The supplement prints its coefficients to three decimals, so several of those checks reconcile strictly rather than through a rounding allowance -- which is stronger evidence than a bare pass. This is what a carefully prepared quantitative paper looks like, and it deserves saying plainly.

It is also worth recording two apparent anomalies that are not anomalies. The within-person negative-affect path is identical, 0.35 (0.06), in all six models, which is the pattern copy-paste detection escalates on; but the six models are fitted to the same 107 participants, neighbouring quantities in the same rows vary at the printed precision, and the supplement's three-decimal version of that path varies in the third decimal across models. They are genuine re-estimations. Likewise, all six columns of supplementary Table S.7 are identical to three decimals across 84 cells -- because the LOC items were administered as a block conditional on having eaten, so the six missingness indicators are one and the same variable. The paper's own Methods supply that explanation.

## Where it does not hold

The defects here are almost entirely about labels, inference and reporting sufficiency rather than about numbers. That distinction matters for how much weight a reader should put on them.

The labelling problem is the one to lead with because it sits in the main results table and repeats six times. It is not a subtle inference: a two-step pathway is printed under a heading reading "Direct effects", the same label is reused a few rows below for different values, and the body text assigns the row's exact standardised coefficients to the path the block is missing. All three checks point the same way, and I re-read the full table grid at source to confirm it. Nothing numeric changes; a reader's understanding of which result is which does.

The inferential problem is more consequential for the conclusions. The paper's second stated aim is that mediation varies across LOC eating dimensions, and the Discussion builds a substantive account on one dimension where the pathway was "not significant", offering explanations for its absence. But that non-significant estimate is compatible with an effect up to 0.099, which is as large as the three effects the paper reports as significant (0.10, 0.09, 0.09). No test of the difference between dimensions is reported, and no smallest effect of interest is stated anywhere, so equivalence cannot be assessed. The first aim -- that emotion dysregulation mediates negative affect's effect on several dimensions -- survives this untouched, and survives multiplicity correction too: three of the four significant pathways clear every standard correction including Benjamini-Yekutieli, which is the right one here given how strongly the LOC dimensions covary. The fourth, difficulties resisting eating at p = 0.026, does not clear any of them, yet appears in the Conclusions on the same footing as the three that do.

Two further items are worth an author's attention rather than a reader's alarm. The emotion dysregulation measurement model is reported with zero degrees of freedom -- it is saturated, so its perfect fit indices are automatic and cannot bear the word "confirmed" that the Methods attach to them; this matters only because that factor is the mediator in every model. And the supplement's stated rule for selecting covariates, R-squared at or above 0.03, excludes at 0.029 the single covariate it was used to include, while not following from the Cohen benchmark cited one sentence earlier. Both look like transcription slips, and either is resolved by a sentence from the authors.

Finally, a cluster of omissions -- no degrees of freedom, no observation-level sample size, and main-table coefficients rounded to two decimals when their magnitude is 0.01 to 0.02 -- means that none of the twelve within-person indirect effects can be independently recomputed from what is printed. Nothing suggests those numbers are wrong; the supplement's three-decimal table shows the authors can report at sufficient precision. It simply means a reader has to take the main table on trust where the supplement lets them check.

The reported statistics in this paper verify. Its central mediation finding for negative affect is robust to correction and I see no reason to doubt it. The claim that mediation differs between LOC eating dimensions is not established by the evidence presented, and the main results table mislabels the coefficient the whole analysis turns on.
